paragraphs: Sullivan County learned it was getting a data center on a Monday morning in late March 2026, when the county commissioners signed a road use agreement and a community enhancement agreement with Heartland Industrial Park. The park covers about 1,000 acres outside New Lebanon, between County Road 400 West and the coal-fired Merom Generating Station, and its backers put the long-term investment at $65 billion over two phases.

County engineer Jerry Netherlain told WTWO the data center would sit on both sides of 200 South, Old State Road 54, with construction starting on the south side. Commissioner Robert Davis said the project would involve seven buildings and two end users who had not been named, and that "there have been certain ones in the county who have been working on it for a year or two." It was, he said, "the first we've told everybody it is a data center."

Under the enhancement agreement the county is to receive $25 million in each phase, and the developer committed $4.5 million to the Brownbaggers School Food Program, the Merom Camp and Retreat Center and Sullivan County Park and Lake. Davis said no local incentives were given. The park's website, as reported at the time, put Phase 1 at $20 billion, two buildings, about 750 peak construction jobs and 125 permanent ones, and Phase 2 at $45 billion.

The developer named locally was Heartland, and the start-up behind it, Potentia; by August the operator presenting the project to residents was the AI cloud company Fluidstack. New Project Media reported that a $5.7 billion bond deal, issued by a joint venture owned 49.9% by Fluidstack and 50.1% by a company related to the investment firm Coatue, with Google guaranteeing Fluidstack's lease, would buy about 140 acres and build two data centers totaling 430MW with an on-site substation, the first 65MW hall due in July 2027.

The ratings firms said the project carries meaningful execution risk, Fitch citing an aggressive construction schedule and limited data center experience on the part of both the sponsor and the contractor.

The fight so far has been about secrecy, roads and jobs more than zoning. Construction began in May, and at a commissioners' meeting that month residents complained that heavy trucks were using roads not permitted for the loads. "They're tearing it up already," one said. Joe Bolk, president of the Wabash Valley Building Trades Council, objected that the first contractor was from Atlanta and brought its own workers and equipment, and Davis said the county's legal team was looking into its options.

At an open house Fluidstack held at the Merom Camp and Retreat Center on August 5, spokesperson Kate Franko said the cooling would be a closed loop that is filled once, that residents' power rates would not rise, and that local unions held nearly $600 million in contracts on the project. The co-op supplier WIN Energy has said the park will pay all costs of its own energy needs.

Merom town councilman John Gettinger told the Tribune-Star the project "seemed to come from out of nowhere" and that the early secrecy had cost trust; Bonnie Boone, who lives near the site, said she still worried about water, electric rates and wildlife. A public Facebook group, Say NO To Data Centers in Sullivan Co, IN, has posted complaints that questions at the open house went unanswered.

The power is the other half of the story. DCD notes that the land came from Hoosier Energy in 2022 and that Hallador Energy, which owns the 1GW Merom plant next door, filed last year to add 515MW of natural gas capacity there. Because Hoosier and WIN Energy are co-ops, a Hoosier representative told New Project Media, their service agreement with the park does not have to be filed with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.

What comes next is the first server building, which Fluidstack hopes to have running around the middle of 2027, and the first enhancement payment, which Franko said was waiting on the county to be ready to receive it. The company has not named its customers.

Morgan County's data center is Google's, though for most of 2025 nobody in Monrovia was allowed to know that. The project began as "Project Louie": at a community meeting on February 10, 2025, the county plan commission presented a rezoning request that the Morgan County Economic Development Corporation had filed for 391 acres on West Keller Hill Road in Monroe Township, just east of Monrovia, on behalf of an unnamed company. The commissioners approved it unanimously on February 18. In May they approved a development agreement under which, the Indianapolis Business Journal reported, the developer pays no local tax on qualified computing equipment for 40 years, on top of a 10-year, 50% abatement on property tax for the data center buildings, with state tax breaks from the Indiana Economic Development Corp. worth up to $42 million over 35 years. The commissioners had signed a non-disclosure agreement keeping the owner's name private. Google confirmed it was the developer in October 2025, a month after it withdrew a data center plan in Franklin Township in Indianapolis in the face of local opposition, and that same month the commissioners rezoned another 158 acres, bringing the site to 549 acres between Keller Hill Road, North Antioch Road, State Road 42 and West Union Church Road.

Google has promised to spend at least $1 billion and to hire 50 people per data center building; current plans call for four. It has not said publicly how much power or water the campus will use, but filings described by the Business Journal show AES Indiana planning a 1,200MW substation on the site, and documents in a case before the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission put water use at about 4 million gallons a day. Run near that capacity for a year, the paper calculated, the campus would use nearly twice the electricity of all AES Indiana's residential customers. Construction began in November 2025. "Nobody here wants to live across the street from an industrial project like this, and yet you are asking me and my neighbors to carry that burden," Sean Walker, who lives across Antioch Road, told the commissioners before their October vote. Gina and Darin Madsen, who bought their Monrovia house two dozen years ago, told the Arnolt Center for Investigative Journalism they had little time to react; "It was already set in stone," Darin Madsen said. Critics have raised energy and water use, noise and property values, and some have sued the county, Indiana Public Media reported.

The site has also become a fight between the county and the town next to it. In March 2026 the Monrovia town council voted 3-2 to begin annexing 890 acres east of town, including the whole Google campus, which would bring the town tax revenue. The county answered by transferring about 600 acres of Google's property to its redevelopment commission under a 10-year lease-back, which under state law cannot be annexed without the county's consent, and in July the redevelopment commission voted unanimously to make the site part of a tax increment financing district. A Google email leaked in late June offered to pay $12 million to double Monrovia's wastewater plant capacity and upgrade its sewers, "contingent upon the town agreeing to end its current annexation process," with a July 3 deadline. "We are being heavily pressured not to annex," council president Tammy Everett told the Morgan County Correspondent.

The power line is what comes next. On September 14, 2026, AES Indiana chose its route for a 10-mile, 345-kilovolt line from a new Antioch substation near Monrovia to a new Blue Bluff substation at the Eagle Valley plant in Martinsville, roughly following Ind. 39 along the edge of Bradford Woods, on towers of 115 to 195 feet and a 200-foot easement. AES says the line is not a dedicated connection for one customer and that Google will pay all of the incremental generation and transmission cost. But a utility analyst for the state's Office of Utility Consumer Counselor testified to the IURC that the project "would not be needed" if no data centers were built in AES territory. AES has not ruled out eminent domain, plans to start construction in fall 2028 and wants the line in service by fall 2029. Autumn Sojka of the Save Morgan County group said her next aim is to see the officials who backed it voted out.
/data-centers/united-states/indiana/morg.unconfirmed: Whether Monrovia accepted Google's $12 million wastewater offer or carried on with annexation after the July 3 deadline was not found in any article that opened. The Correspondent's TIF story is paywalled after its first paragraph; only the unanimous vote is used. WTHR's story on the 550-acre plan returned Access Denied. The lawsuit against the county is mentioned only as IPM reported it; its claims and status were not read.

paragraphs: Rapides Parish's data center is Delta Forge 1, a $3.6 billion AI campus that Applied Digital Corp. is building on about 300 acres near I-49 just south of the town of Boyce. Gov. Jeff Landry announced it at the England Airpark community center on May 26, 2026, though site work had begun in January. The first phase is two buildings with about 300MW of critical IT load, a figure that excludes cooling and lighting, and Applied Digital describes it as a long-term campus under a 15-year initial lease with three five-year renewals. The company, which is based in Dallas, has not named the tenant. Its application to the England Economic and Industrial Development District covers 672.52 acres, and construction plans KALB obtained through records requests show schematics for two or three more "future" buildings; the company told the station only two are planned for now. Operations are expected to start in mid-2027, with 200 permanent jobs at or above 150% of the state's average wage and more than 1,000 construction jobs at the peak.

Instead of property taxes, Applied Digital will make payments in lieu of taxes under a term sheet KALB obtained: $27.4 million in the first year, falling in steps to $19.4 million a year by years 22 to 25, plus $18 million a year for three years to regional taxing bodies and community development. The company also escapes state sales tax on data center equipment under Act 730 of 2024. Cleco will supply the power over a 230,000-volt transmission line, and says the campus will be its largest customer ever. Cleco chief commercial officer Shane Hilton said the company does not expect any rate increase from the project and that the data center will pay for the substations and transmission it needs, subject to a prudency review at the Public Service Commission. The Louisiana Illuminator noted that neither Cleco nor state officials have said anything about building a new power plant.

The environmental record is only partly public. Filings with the state Department of Environmental Quality, LDEQ, show each of the two buildings will hold 96 diesel-fired emergency generators, with 32 diesel storage tanks, under a synthetic minor source air permit, and stormwater from construction may be discharged into Bertrand Bayou. On May 27 the department cited the site for failing to control particulate emissions after residents complained about dust. Applied Digital says the closed-loop cooling needs about 866,000 gallons per building to fill, and the Rapides Island Water Association has committed 1,200 to 4,800 gallons a day after that; the company has not given noise figures. Many power and water documents were withheld from KALB as trade secrets. Elsewhere in Louisiana, Meta is building its Hyperion campus in Richland Parish, Hut 8 a $10 billion campus in West Feliciana Parish, and Amazon campuses are planned in Caddo and Bossier parishes.

The anger in Boyce, a town of about 1,000, has been mostly about secrecy. Records obtained by the Gulf States Newsroom and Type Investigations show that at least five state senators, the parish assessor and every member of the development district's board signed non-disclosure agreements under the code names "Project Lightning" and "Project Pixel"; the board approved the deal on April 23 with little discussion. At a June 23 town hall in a Boyce gym, residents jeered when officials said a third-party environmental study would not be released. "Our politicians were elected to represent us, not to represent industry," resident Robert Maddox told the board. The district's executive director, Ralph Hennessy, called the critics "a vocal minority" and told NPR, "NDAs are not illegal, OK?" Applied Digital chief executive Wes Cummins said he would "love to be able to get away from the NDA part because it just feels sneaky to people."
/data-centers/united-states/louisiana/ra.unconfirmed: The Advocate's announcement story opened but only its photo captions were read; nothing from its body is used. KALB's May story lists $77 million to parish government and other cumulative payments that do not reconcile with the PILOT term sheet KALB later obtained; only the term sheet figures are used. The outcome of the Public Service Commission review of Cleco's service to the site was not found. The tenant is unnamed. No story after August 2026 was found.

paragraphs: West Feliciana Parish's data center is Hut 8's River Bend campus, under construction off La. 964 near St. Francisville, next to Entergy's River Bend nuclear plant. The parish approved the rezoning in January 2025 for what was then a $2.5 billion project, and Hut 8 bought the 611-acre tract that February. The first phase, two 450,000-square-foot buildings, will need 300 megawatts of power, enough for about 54,000 homes a year, GovTech reported, and Hut 8 aims to be fully operational by the third quarter of 2027.

Parish President Kenny Havard negotiated with Hut 8 directly, skipping the state's economic development office and any non-disclosure agreements. Hut 8 donated its site to a new parish Industrial Development Board, which leases it back for rent equal to the property tax its GPUs would otherwise owe, worth up to $90 million a year from mid-2027, split among the parish, the sheriff and the schools. "It's going to be our next oil boom," Havard said. Hut 8 is also paying $16 million for a new water well and fire hydrants for the parish.

Residents near the site say they can already hear construction, and Hut 8 said in July 2026 a noise study would conclude within weeks; no result has been published. The company will truck in at least 2 million gallons of water for a closed cooling loop but won't say how much the site needs overall. Entergy Louisiana says it has enough power for the plant and residents, though Logan Burke of the Alliance for Affordable Energy told WBRZ "there hasn't been much transparency about this project." Havard says future phases could triple the site and need 1,000 megawatts or more.

A Denver developer called Tract wants to put a 900MW data center campus, Tuckahoe Technology Park, on about 870 acres at the eastern edge of Goochland, bounded by Hockett Road, Patterson Avenue, Route 288 and the Mosaic at West Creek neighborhood, a 55-and-over community of more than 500 homes. Tract is under contract to buy the land, 11 parcels owned by members of the Haddock, Stern and Arenstein families. The concept shows seven development areas and around 12 buildings totaling about 3 million square feet, most 60 feet tall and some up to 80. Tract projects $400 million in real property tax and more than $600 million in personal property tax over the first 20 years, $3 billion in construction and 350 permanent jobs. Tract usually prepares land and power and then sells sites to other companies to build on, and no end user has been named; its application refers to "a restriction on end user to ensure County receives anticipated tax revenues" without saying what that is.

The campus is the first test of the Technology Overlay District that supervisors approved 4-1 in November 2025, over heavy opposition. The district runs about five miles along Route 288 and covers roughly 4,400 acres, most of it in the West Creek Business Park, where data centers are allowed by right; it also allows a small modular nuclear reactor or a gas peaking plant with a conditional use permit. After residents flooded the county with objections, the county carved out the 900 acres near Mosaic and Richmond Country Club as "TOD West," where data centers need a conditional use permit and public hearings, saying it had learned of private talks between a developer and the landowners only after they had happened. A group of residents has sued the supervisors and planning commissioners over how the district was adopted.

Opposition to Tract's plan has been loud. At a Tract community meeting at Goochland High School on July 23, 2026, dozens of residents in red shirts protested outside. "We want to make sure that everyone understands that we don't want data centers in Goochland," said resident Cynthia Haas. Residents also asked about diesel generators near homes, noise and where transmission lines would run. In its formal application on August 5, Tract committed to non-evaporative, air-cooled closed-loop cooling that it says cuts water use by about 95%, lowered its proposed noise limit at the property line from 55 to 52 dBA, and set generator areas 1,000 feet from Mosaic homes, some of which sit 70 to 80 feet from the northern property line.

The application is under completeness review and would go to the Goochland Planning Commission in October 2026 at the earliest, then to the Board of Supervisors for a final vote. Tract has already lost once nearby: Hanover County supervisors voted 4-3 in late May 2026 to reject its Mountain Road Technology Park.

Frederick County has one operating data center, the 6-megawatt Middletown Data Center on Valley Pike, but is now deciding whether to allow any more. The Board of Supervisors held public hearings on September 23, 2026 on an ordinance amendment that would remove data centers from every zoning district in the county, which would make Frederick the first Virginia locality to do so if it passes, and on a permit for Winchester Gateway, a 72-acre, three-building project in Kernstown. The hearings were scheduled for that date; no result has been published.

The push came from residents who filled meetings over water, noise, traffic and health, including a May 7 forum at James Wood High School that drew hundreds. The Planning Commission has recommended denying both pending projects: Equus Capital Partners' 220-acre Virginia Technology Park near Clear Brook, and Winchester Gateway, whose developer capped water use and added buffers but still would not say how many megawatts the site needs. Neither project has its own row in the county's table above yet.

County officials are fighting a proposed power line too, setting aside $250,000 to oppose Valley Link's planned Valley North transmission route, which could cross Frederick and neighboring Clarke County. "We're not a highway. This has got to stop," board chairman John Jewell said. Three sitting supervisors, including Jewell, face independent anti-data-center challengers in November special elections.

Microsoft owns the Person County Mega Park, about 1,350 acres of fields, forest and creek in Woodsdale Township on the Virginia line, seven miles north of Roxboro, and plans to build a data center there. The company bought the land for about $27 million in October 2024, but it and the county did not confirm the site would hold a data center until February 2026. County Manager Katherine Cathey has said Microsoft plans to begin permitting later in 2026; no size, power figure, investment or job count has been published.

How the deal was done is the local controversy. Records show the county's economic development director, county manager and county attorney worked under non-disclosure agreements on "Project Energy" from May 2024. Commissioners rezoned the land that August without naming the client, then voted 4-1 in September to close a stretch of Country Club Road through the site without telling residents the closure was Microsoft's condition of sale. "It takes EMS 11 minutes to go around now," said Tina Clayton, who lives nearby. Microsoft said in March 2026 it would stop using NDAs with local governments; the economic development director was fired the same month.

Water and power are what residents keep asking about. Microsoft says it will use air-cooled chillers on a closed loop, pay its own way on electricity, and replenish more water than it uses; Sierra Club member Olive Burress said those commitments are voluntary. Roxboro council member Kendra Coggins said, "It feels like we got a lot of canned responses." Duke Energy is meanwhile adding gas generation and converting two coal units at its nearby Roxboro plant, and the county's economic development chair told state regulators in 2025 that a data center was the reason for the extra capacity.

What comes next is Microsoft's first permit filing, which will show how big the campus is and how much water and power it needs. Residents sent Microsoft 21 questions in August 2025 on water, power, emergency access and timelines; asked whether it would reply, Microsoft pointed to a blog post.

Kings Mountain has paused new data centers until late August 2027. The City Council adopted a 182-day moratorium on February 24, 2026, and on August 25 voted to extend it by a full year while it writes rules; another company was seeking approval for a data center when the pause began. The city is already home to T5 Data Centers' Kings Mountain campus.

The first vote was 5-2. Planning director Henry Earle told the council the city had "zero standards relating to data centers" beyond ordinary zoning, and the city's findings called the chance of a proposal "extremely high." Councilmember Annie Thombs, who moved the pause, said: "For the safety of all citizens, I'm not going to get caught up in money." Scott Neisler and Tyler Fletcher voted no; Fletcher worried the pause "may push a project away that may not return."

Water was the top complaint among residents protesting outside City Hall. "I don't think they need to build nothing until they take care of our power bills, our water, and our taxes," said George Hammett Jr. The draft standards cover lot sizes, setbacks, screening, lighting, noise and whether the city can supply electricity, gas, water and sewer.

T5's campus is not new: in 2013 T5 signed a tenant for half of a 150,000-square-foot building there in a $70 million deal, and the campus already held data centers for AT&T, Walt Disney Co. and Wipro.

North Ostrobothnia's data center story is Google in Muhos, a municipality of about 9,000 people. Google bought land there in 2024, and in early March 2026 the municipal council approved the Pyhänsivu-Leppiniemi local detailed plan, which reserves more than 600 hectares for data centres and other industry with nearly two million square metres of permitted building space. Current plans call for nine server halls. On September 9, 2026, Google announced that Muhos is one of four Finnish sites, with Hamina, Kajaani and Vaala, in a €13 billion, two-year investment in data centres and supporting infrastructure that it called its largest single investment in Europe; Prime Minister Petteri Orpo welcomed it. Google has not given a megawatt figure for Muhos.

Work is already visible. Forest clearance at the Pyhänsivu site began in the spring, and up to 30,000 loads of crushed stone were expected by the end of November, delivered around the clock roughly every five minutes. Tapani Ervasti, chair of the municipal executive board, compared the volume with that used for the Hailuoto bridge, which took 18 months to move where Muhos is doing it in under six, called the announcement "an enormous thing for Muhos," and estimated 2,000 to 3,000 construction workers and up to 1,000 jobs once running. Under a land use agreement reported by Yle, Google is to pay the municipality €26 million once the plan takes legal effect and the municipality starts building roads and utilities to the site.

The plan is not yet in force. One appeal has been lodged with the administrative court by a private individual, who argues, according to Yle, that the plan did not adequately study the effects on nature and suspects that the €26 million agreement steered the zoning; the appeal delays both the works and the payment. Municipal manager Kimmo Hinno declined to comment on it. In September the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation told the news agency STT it suspected illegal logging at the Muhos and Kajaani sites, where trees were felled before environmental impact assessments were complete, and asked for construction in Muhos to be suspended until the assessment is done; the Permits and Supervision Agency has opened an investigation. Google said the felling complied fully with the Forest Act. Association chair Hanna Halmeenpää said it was either gross incompetence by Google's Finnish project company, Tuike Finland Oy, or gross disregard for Finnish law.

Google has also promised local projects in the host municipalities, from public saunas and docks to heat pumps for low-income households, and to donate its timber proceeds locally. Anna Hannula, a senior lecturer at Tampere University, warned that such a large private role in a small municipality could create dependencies and pressure on democratic decision-making. Muhos sits in a wider cluster of big projects along the border with Kainuu, including billion-euro schemes in Kajaani and Utajärvi. The next decisions are the administrative court's ruling on the appeal and the environmental impact assessment; Ervasti has said Google has not slowed the project despite the appeal.
/data-centers/finland/north-ostrobothnia.unconfirmed: Remarks by Finnish speakers are given as reported speech because the English outlets carried translations; the Yle appeal story was read in Finnish. Google's capacity, power supply and investment figure for Muhos alone were not found. When the administrative court will rule is not known. Yle's April story said Google had not yet made a final investment decision; the September announcement names Muhos but its text does not say construction of buildings has been approved.

paragraphs: Kanta-Häme's data center is QTS's planned campus in Forssa, in the Ratasmäki and Rytökallio industrial area, next to a Fingrid national grid power line. QTS is owned by Blackstone, which signed a preliminary agreement with the city in March 2025 for more than 100 hectares; Forssa's mayor, Jari Kesäniemi, said at the time that it could become one of the largest data center projects in Europe, and Yle reported a maximum power draw of up to 450MW. The city says it has since completed the land sales, for about €4 million, which it says matches or exceeds outside valuations. QTS describes it as its first campus in Finland, on a 150-hectare site, and expects more than 300 operational jobs at full build-out and more than 500 construction jobs at peak. The local development partner is Brunswick Real Estate.

The project has cleared the main local hurdles without a fight on the record. The detailed plan for the area took legal effect in December 2025 with no appeals lodged by the deadline, Kesäniemi told Yle. On July 23, 2026, the city granted the first building permit to QTS's Finnish company, Green 3 Finland Oy, for a plot of almost 44 hectares at Masmalokatu 1: a three-storey building of almost 60,000 square metres with nine data halls of 9MW each, 81MW in total, plus a substation, service and guard buildings and a waste-heat recovery system. Space is reserved for two more data center buildings whose permits will be sought later, and Fingrid is to build a switching station in the south-west corner. The permit allowed preparatory work to start before it took legal effect in early September, against a €300,000 guarantee to cover restoration if the project stopped. QTS says phase one construction is tentatively set for 2027 and that it will use a closed-loop, water-free cooling system.

Forssa is one of several large projects in Finland's data center boom. Google announced in September 2026 a €13 billion, two-year investment in Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, and TikTok has planned a €1 billion, 150MW data center in Kouvola. QTS held supplier briefings in Forssa on August 25, 2026 and ran a training open day with the regional vocational college the next day.

The concerns documented are ecological rather than political. The state permits and supervision agency, Lupa- ja valvontavirasto, found in the environmental impact assessment that without mitigation the project could have significant negative effects in some respects. Flying squirrels, moor frogs and a protected dragonfly, the täpläkorento, live on the site: the flying squirrels' core territory is to be kept with a buffer zone and extra trees, and a pond used by the frogs and dragonflies will be fenced and its water level monitored during construction. Stormwater will be run through settling and retention basins. Forssa's lead building inspector, Jukka Laaksonen, told Yle the permit decision ran so long it was "like a novel." How much electricity the full campus will ultimately draw, and when Blackstone makes its final investment decision on the later buildings, have not been published.
/data-centers/finland/kanta-hame/.unconfirmed: Yle stories and the city's project page were read in Finnish; remarks are given as reported speech except Laaksonen's phrase, translated. The 450MW figure is the maximum Yle reported in March 2025; the permitted first building is 81MW. Yle linked a story saying operations could begin in 2029, which did not open and is not used. No opposition or appeal was found; the page does not say there was none.

paragraphs: The Swedish company EcoDataCenter is building its biggest campus yet at the former Kvarnsveden paper mill in Borlänge, where it broke ground in September 2025; the first phase, due in 2027, is set at 250 megawatts of power, with room for more than 360. In late August 2026 it signed to buy 52 hectares from Smedjebacken municipality for a third Dalarna campus of up to 150 megawatts; building and environmental permits are expected in early 2027, and construction can start once they are final.

EcoDataCenter opened its first data center in Falun in 2019, and that campus could reach 80 megawatts. Its customers include the U.S. AI cloud company CoreWeave, which said in 2024 it would put Nvidia chips in Falun rather than build its own Swedish site, along with Mistral AI and DeepL. At Kvarnsveden, site manager Johan Appelberg told Lokalt i Dalarna the build would employ 400 to 500 people; Borlänge's council sold the company a third of the old mill for 400 million kronor.

The local argument is about electricity. EcoDataCenter's consultation notice for Kvarnsveden gave a maximum supplied power of 760 megawatts, with backup diesel generators, and a 2024 letter in Borlänge Tidning said that is more than one of the shut reactors at Oskarshamn or Barsebäck produced. A debate article in the same paper this year said Kvarnsveden may suit a data center but urged the city-owned Borlänge Energi to publish how the connection will affect grid fees and district heating.

Skåne's data center is Microsoft's in Staffanstorp, west of the town center, part of the Sweden Central cloud region with Microsoft's sites near Gävle and Sandviken that opened in late 2021. Microsoft still runs it, but on August 26, 2022 it dropped plans to expand it and said it would look for a larger site elsewhere in southern Sweden.

The fight was over diesel generators. Sydsvenskan reported that the building's original permit described it as a warehouse, not a data center, and that only once it was finished did Microsoft apply to the county board for an environmental permit for diesel backup generators, which the paper showed would release harmful air pollution. SVT reported that the county board had taken the view that the application should not be approved.

Microsoft then withdrew the application, which covered backup power for a facility with 70 megawatts of supplied power. It said it would keep running and expanding Staffanstorp using only the generators already there, by adjusting which services the site offers. Communications head Andreas Wingren told SVT local reaction had not affected the decision and that Skåne remained important to the company, but that it was too early to say which towns might host the new site.

Amazon Web Services runs data centers in Eskilstuna and Katrineholm, two of the three sites behind its Stockholm cloud region, and is expanding both. In Eskilstuna's logistics park, AWS has applied for a building permit to add 88,000 square meters in three buildings on its 33-hectare property, next to the roughly 20,000-square-meter center that opened in 2018. The third site in the region is in Västerås, in neighboring Västmanland.

Asked about power, Kjell Andersson, chief executive of the city utility Eskilstuna Energi och Miljö, told E-kuriren that AWS does not use all the capacity it booked when it first arrived, leaving room for the expansion. In Katrineholm, AWS says the steel for its new building came entirely from scrap melted in electric furnaces run on carbon-free power.

Two other projects are under way in the county. In Eskilstuna, Scandinavian Data Centers is turning the Ärnaberget rock caverns near Torshälla, where aircraft engines were once built, into a 2 billion kronor data center, ScandiDC I, due for tenants in the fourth quarter of 2026, with waste heat for the city's district heating. In Strängnäs, Brookfield plans an AI data center that Byggindustrin says would be the largest foreign direct investment in Sweden ever at full size; construction was planned for 2026 if the power supply can be solved first.

The one data center planned in the North Denmark Region is Prime Data Centers' campus on Energivej in Sæby, south of Frederikshavn. Prime, based in Santa Clara, California, announced it in February 2023 as its first data center outside the US: three buildings with 12 halls, about 100,000 square meters over three stories and 124 megawatts of power, on land then covered by solar panels. Prime gave no construction date, and its newest Danish plan, announced in March 2026, is a larger campus in Esbjerg.

Frederikshavn had the site ready before it had a builder. "The local plan and everything else has been in place. The only thing we were missing was an investor," Mayor Birgit Hansen told the regional paper Nordjyske in 2023. Under a deal with the local heating company, Sæby Fjernvarme, the plant would send cooling water to the data center and take it back warm to heat homes in the town of about 9,000 people, and Prime said the campus would run on 100 percent renewable power.

Both data centers mapped in the Capital Region are in Ballerup, on the western edge of Copenhagen. atNorth's DEN01 opened its first phase in the last quarter of 2025 after a 12-month build and offers 30 megawatts of power for computers, the company says. Digital Realty runs its Copenhagen campus nearby, where it began building a third data center, CPH3, planned at up to 14.4 megawatts.

DEN01's waste heat is meant to warm local homes. atNorth has signed a deal with Vestforbrænding, Denmark's largest waste-to-energy company, to feed the data center's surplus heat into its district heating network, enough for more than 8,000 homes starting in 2028. "For many years, we have talked about surplus heat from data centers being part of the future," Vestforbrænding's chief executive, Steen Neuchs Vedel, said. "Now the future is here."

Any new data center here now waits on the power grid. On March 2, 2026, the state grid operator Energinet stopped signing new grid connections nationwide, with about 60 gigawatts of requests queued against a national peak demand of about 7 gigawatts; data centers made up about 14 gigawatts of that. The pause ended June 3, but Energinet will not decide on new large connections until its first round under stricter rules, expected in the last three months of 2026, and warned many new customers could wait five to 10 years.

Google plans its first self-run data center in France on 195 hectares of the Ozans business zone at Étrechet, a village about 10 kilometers southeast of Châteauroux. Through a subsidiary, Tricolore Computing, it signed a five-year promise to buy the land on July 5, 2025, for a campus of about ten buildings needing more than 500 megawatts of power. Construction is meant to start in 2029, Châteauroux Métropole president Gil Avérous said in June 2026, and a public consultation run by France's National Commission for Public Debate is expected in October 2026.

The project has split Étrechet's town hall. On September 15, 2026, Mayor Florence Laurent resigned over "a disagreement on how opinions about the Google project on our territory are taken into account," after three deputy mayors and a councilor had already quit. She said the builders should make firm commitments on visual impact, PFAS chemicals, falling home values and road traffic, and that at a September 9 council meeting "we were told the project would go ahead." Avérous says every Ozans project has been approved by Étrechet and the other towns in the metropolitan area.

Farmer Emmanuel de Saint Pol, whose land at Ozans was taken in 2012 for a Chinese investor's project that never came, told the Multinationals Observatory: "I'm mostly just tired of it." Jérémie Godet, the regional council's vice president for climate, says he is "convinced their strategy is to target regions where opposition is weak."

Power is the main hurdle. The department's high-voltage lines are full, and the grid operator RTE plans to double the 400,000-volt line from the Éguzon dam to Marmagne, with work not expected before 2032. Nearby in Buzançais, the Val-de-l'Indre community has sold 10 hectares to Decknet for a data center due to open in 2027.

Marseille is France's second data center hub after Paris because of the undersea internet cables that land there. Digital Realty runs four data centers in the port, MRS1 to MRS4, and is building a fifth, MRS5, on the site of the old Saint-Louis sugar silo, due to open at the end of 2026. In March 2026 the town of Bouc-Bel-Air granted it a permit for MRS6: a €700 million, 50-megawatt data center in a former Decathlon warehouse in the Chabauds zone, with work to start in 2026 and servers online in early 2028.

MRS5 made data centers a public argument in Marseille. In September 2024 the collective Le nuage était sous nos pieds, formed by La Quadrature du Net, Technopolice and the Gammares group, held a press conference opposite the silo. Patrick Robert, who represents neighborhood committees in the north of the city, said MRS5 would use 241 million kilowatt-hours a year, "the equivalent of the 13th arrondissement of Marseille," and doubted the grid could also power the quays so docked ships can switch off their engines. Deputy mayor Sébastien Barles called for a moratorium on new data centers in the city.

In Bouc-Bel-Air, the residents' association of the south of town gathered nearly 2,000 signatures against MRS6 over noise and power use. The inquiry commissioner gave a favorable opinion with reservations on landscaping and architecture.

South Korea's national AI computing center is under construction at the Solaseado Data Center Park in Haenam County; the science ministry broke ground on August 3, 2026. It is being built and run by Korea AI Computing Center Co. (CoreAIC), set up in June 2026 by the government, the National Growth Fund and a Samsung SDS-led group that includes Naver Cloud, Kakao and KT. Plans call for 2.5 trillion won of investment, 15,000 advanced chips by 2028 and 50,000 by 2030, with full operation in 2028.

CoreAIC says it has applied to KEPCO, the state utility, for power and is laying a water pipeline. Haenam's pitch is renewable power: a 98-megawatt solar complex already runs at Solaseado, with 5.4 gigawatts planned by 2030, and the county is setting up a residents' fund so locals share in energy income. In July 2026 the county council passed an ordinance backing AI, chip and data industries, which the county tied to the computing center and about 17 trillion won of AI data center investment.

The second project is SK's part of OpenAI's Stargate plan for Korea. In October 2025 the government said OpenAI's joint ventures with Samsung SDS and SK Telecom would build two data centers with an initial 20 megawatts. On February 11, 2026 the science minister said construction would start in March, but SK Telecom told Reuters it was still in talks on a site in southwestern Korea, with timing under review. The Seoul Economic Daily has named Solaseado as a leading candidate; no site has been announced.

Microsoft runs two data centers in Busan's International Industrial Logistics City in Gangseo-gu and is preparing a third, larger one. Edaily reported on June 1, 2026 that Microsoft's Korean data center company, 5673 Korea, plans a 125-megawatt building on land in the Mieum area it bought from the city's development corporation in 2025. Construction is scheduled to start in October 2026 and finish in October 2031.

The first Busan data center opened in April 2020; the second, larger Miumsandan building was unveiled on September 23, 2024 with Mayor Park Heong-joon. Edaily said the two together total 85 megawatts of power and put the third building's cost at more than 2 trillion won. It reported that Microsoft was looking to lease neighboring land to speed up construction, and that it plans to add more than 100 megawatts beyond that once power supply is settled, for a cluster of over 400 megawatts at Mieum.

Power is the local question. In January 2024 the Busan broadcaster KNN reported that the city's planned complex of five data centers in Eco Delta City, on 177,000 square meters and asking for up to 360 megawatts, would share a new Singangseo substation of about 1,000 megawatts that must also serve the Mieum industrial area. A KEPCO official told KNN the substation's current capacity would struggle to cover those loads. The city said adding transformers would solve it and was negotiating with the industry ministry and KEPCO; the substation is due by December 2027.

Princeton Digital Group is building its first South Korean data center, SE1, in Incheon's Bupyeong district: a nine-story, 48-megawatt building on 11,000 square meters, a $700 million project due to open in early 2028. The real estate firm ESR, which calls the building KR1, is putting up the shell with Wide Creek Asset Management and said in November 2025 that construction was starting that week. PDG says the site's power is fully contracted.

Bupyeong has been through one data center fight already. SEL2, a data center built by SK ecoplant and Singapore's Digital Edge at 422 Cheongcheon-dong in the Bupyeong national industrial complex, needed a 1,985-meter underground high-voltage line from KEPCO's Galsan substation. When residents of the Ian apartments in Galsan-dong learned in August 2023 that the route passed about 200 meters away, the district halted 600 meters of the work. Residents wanted the line buried deeper than the 3 meters offered and radiation monitors at three spots.

The district let digging resume in February 2024, telling the Kyeongin Ilbo it would probably lose if the developer sued for tens of billions of won in damages. SEL2 opened in August 2024, with a second phase due to start in 2025. KEPCO's planned New Bupyeong converter station in Galsan-dong, a roughly 250 billion won project meant to relieve overloads on Incheon's grid, was turned down by the district's building committee from 2022 through 2024 over residents' objections. In March 2025 KEPCO said it could not yet set a start date.
